settings.heading: 7 Things to Check Before Buying a Pre-Owned Resin Statue
settings.intro: Buying a pre-owned resin statue well comes down to seven checks: identify the exact statue, studio and edition; ask for photographs of the actual item; look for damage and repairs; confirm every component is present; verify the original packaging; plan for dimensions, weight and delivery; and total the real cost including what protection you have if it arrives wrong. Episode 001 follows three collectors making every one of those checks the hard way.

settings.title: Identify the studio, scale, edition and authenticity evidence
settings.text: Ask for the studio name, the scale, the edition size and any certificate or numbered plaque. Many resin statues come from small studios producing short runs, so a vague listing is often a listing the seller cannot substantiate. If a piece carries a certificate, ask for a photograph of it rather than a description.

settings.title: Request clear photographs of the actual statue
settings.text: Studio renders are made before production and show the piece at its best. What you are buying is one specific example that has been owned and displayed. Ask for photographs of that example, taken recently, in daylight, from several angles — and treat reluctance as information.

settings.title: Inspect chips, cracks, paintwork and previous repairs
settings.text: Resin chips rather than flexes, so damage tends to be at thin points: fingers, hair, weapons, flame and cloth edges. Look for colour breaks, a seam that does not line up, or a glossy patch where matte paint should be. A disclosed repair is a negotiation; an undisclosed one is a reason to ask what else was not mentioned.

settings.title: Confirm all parts, accessories and assembly joints
settings.text: These statues arrive in parts and are assembled. Swap hands, alternate heads, effect pieces, light units and power leads all go missing over time. Ask for the original parts list and a photograph of everything laid out, then check each join is sound rather than merely held together.

settings.title: Check original packaging and protective inserts
settings.text: A boxed piece is generally worth more than an unboxed one, and the moulded inserts are the only safe way to move a statue again. A box with a crushed corner is cosmetic; missing inserts are a real problem, because a replacement rarely fits the contours.

settings.title: Verify dimensions, weight, safe transportation and delivery costs
settings.text: Bases are often the widest part, and a statue that fits your shelf on paper can still be too deep for it. Get height, width, depth and weight before you commit, then ask how it will actually travel. A courier network is not designed for a fragile object of this size and value.

settings.title: Check total price, seller credibility, return terms and buyer protection
settings.text: Add delivery, any assembly and any insurance to the headline price before comparing. Then establish what happens if it arrives damaged or not as described: who collects it, who pays, and how long you have. A seller who will put that in writing is telling you something useful.

settings.heading: The seven checks in full
settings.body: The story above is fiction. These checks are not — they are the questions worth asking of any pre-owned resin statue, wherever you buy it.

settings.heading: How we handle this
settings.body:
Every piece in our One Piece collection is photographed as it stands, with its condition described as we find it and its original packaging listed where it is included. Delivery is priced by postcode before you add anything to a basket, and the Hassle-Free Handover Guarantee sets out what happens if a piece arrives damaged, missing a listed part or not as described.

Chasing a specific statue, studio or edition? Tell us what you’re after and we’ll let you know if one reaches us.
